hints: Is it enough that each node is bigger than its left child and smaller than its right child? Try to build a tree where that holds but a deeper node is on the wrong side.
Pass a range (low, high) down the recursion: every node must lie strictly inside the range set by its ancestors. Going left tightens high; going right tightens low.

1. Call check(root, -∞, +∞) (use long bounds).
  2. A null node is valid.
  3. If node.val is not strictly between low and high, return false.
  4. Check the left child with range (low, node.val).
  5. Check the right child with range (node.val, high).

approaches.name: Brute force
approaches.idea: For every node, scan its whole left subtree and right subtree to confirm all values are smaller / larger.

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.idea: One DFS carrying the allowed open interval for each node (or an in-order walk checking values strictly increase).

explain: In [10,4,15,null,null,12,20], 10 gets range (−∞, ∞), 4 gets (−∞, 10), 15 gets (10, ∞), 12 gets (10, 15) and 20 gets (15, ∞) — all fit, so the answer is true. In sample 2 the node 8 sits under 15 and gets range (10, 15); 8 is not above 10, so the answer is false, even though 8 < 15 looks fine locally. Use long bounds so values equal to Integer.MIN_VALUE or MAX_VALUE are handled, and use strict comparisons because duplicates are not allowed.
recognize: "All values in the left subtree smaller" → validate with an inherited (low, high) range, not just parent–child checks.
